name: cjson.cpp
workload: Parsing/serializing a corpus of real-world JSON documents (64KB-5MB: github_events, twitter, citm_catalog, canada, numbers, etc.) with cjson.cpp's index/tape parser vs nlohmann::json 3.12.0's owning-tree parser, RapidJSON 1.1.0, Boost.JSON 1.90.0, simdjson, and yyjson, on the project's own corpus_vs benchmark
claimed_speedup: vs simdjson-dom(warm) (as printed on page): 1.18x GB/s on 64KB (2.69 vs 2.29 GB/s), 1.11x on 1MB (2.52 vs 2.27 GB/s), ~0.99x (essentially tied, slightly behind) on twitter.json and 5MB. vs nlohmann::json 3.12.0: ~31x faster parse throughput on 1MB (2.52 vs 0.08 GB/s) and ~25x faster on extract-dom of twitter.json (2.02 vs 0.08 GB/s) (both derived from page data). vs yyjson (serialize, as printed on page): 2.13x on twitter.json (2.33 vs 1.09 GB/s), 3.16x on 1MB (2.21 vs 0.70 GB/s), 3.12x on 5MB (2.11 vs 0.68 GB/s)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.1.1 20260515; every contender built -O3 -march=native -flto -ffat-lto-objects, bench TU adds -Ofast -std=c++26
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700U, kernel 7.1.7-200.fc44.x86_64, taskset -c 0, medians of 7 runs
tradeoffs: Depends on a custom 'micron' core library instead of the traditional C++ STL/glibc (README states 'no support for the traditional C++ Standard Library'); requires C++26; cjson is an index/tape parser (strings not materialized, lazy unescape) so its output shape differs from nlohmann's fully-materialized owning tree.
caveats: The cjson-vs-nlohmann numbers compare different parser categories (cjson's index/tape parse vs nlohmann's full owning-tree parse) shown in separate chart bands on the README, not a same-band apples-to-apples row; the ~25-31x figures are computed by dividing across those two bands. Repo is about 6 weeks old, 2 stars, single author, not independently reproduced by a third party. On some documents (twitter.json, 5MB) cjson is roughly tied with or slightly behind simdjson-dom.

name: DAW JSON Link
baseline: RapidJSON (also compared against simdjson and C++ Boost/PropertyTree in the same suite)
workload: kostya/benchmarks cross-language JSON parsing shootout: parse a generated JSON coordinate dataset and compute a checksum/distance, timed end-to-end, run on two separate machines
claimed_speedup: Fastest of ~20 language/library entries on both machines (derived from page's raw seconds, not printed as ratios): 2017 MacBook Air (Core i5-5350U) -- DAW JSON Link 0.19s vs RapidJSON 0.53s (2.8x faster), vs simdjson 0.31s (1.6x faster), vs C++ Boost 10.42s (55x faster); Linux (Core i7-7500U, gcc 9.2.1) -- DAW JSON Link 0.11s vs RapidJSON 0.26s (2.4x faster), vs simdjson 0.21s (1.9x faster), vs C++ Boost 4.14s (38x faster)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1 stated for the Linux run; compiler unspecified for the MacBook Air run
hardware: Intel Core i7-7500U @2.70GHz, 32GB RAM, Linux 5.3.0-29 (one table); Intel Core i5-5350U @1.80GHz, 8GB RAM, 2017 MacBook Air (other table)
tradeoffs: Requires describing the JSON schema at compile time via reflection/data-member mapping rather than a drop-in mutable DOM like nlohmann::json; heavy template metaprogramming increases compile times; header-only.
caveats: kostya/benchmarks hardware/compiler are dated (gcc 9.2.1, 2015-2017 era CPUs); the benchmark's own README notes each machine ran a different dataset so cross-machine numbers are only relatively comparable, not absolute; results are as archived in daw_json_link's own docs, not independently re-run recently. C++ Boost figures in this table are Boost.PropertyTree, not Boost.JSON.

name: utl::json (part of the UTL header-only library collection)
baseline: nlohmann::json (also PicoJSON; beats RapidJSON on serialization tasks only, loses to it on most parsing tasks)
workload: Parsing and serializing minimized/prettified JSON test files (strings.json, numbers.json, twitter.json, apache_builds.json, database.json) with a benchmark harness comparing utl::json, nlohmann, PicoJSON, and RapidJSON
claimed_speedup: ~2.2-2.4x faster parsing than nlohmann::json on twitter.json (402.89 vs 182.76 op/s) and apache_builds.json (2134.76 vs 881.03 op/s); ~1.9-2.4x faster serializing than nlohmann on the same files (e.g. twitter.json serialize: 834.42 vs 440.27 op/s); with a custom flat-map object type (not the library's default std::map), the author reports it 'beat RapidJSON on all serializing tasks' and closed most of the parsing gap on object-heavy database.json (all ratios derived from the page's relative-% table, which the page itself reports directly as percentages)
tradeoffs: Uses std::map for JSON objects by default, which the author states is the main performance weak point on object-heavy documents; JSON values map onto standard containers (std::map/std::vector/std::string) for STL interoperability rather than a custom optimized container, trading some speed for simplicity.
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags are stated on the benchmark page itself (only relative %, ms/op, op/s and an error% from what looks like a nanobench/ankerl-style harness) -- self-reported, partial methodology. Not a universal win: on numbers.json and apache_builds.json, RapidJSON actually beats utl::json on parsing (128-172% relative i.e. faster); the win is consistent only vs nlohmann and PicoJSON.

name: Tachyon.JSON v6
baseline: nlohmann::json (also compared against simdjson and Glaze)
workload: Parsing a 25MB synthetic large-array JSON document and canada.json (geographic coordinate corpus) with CPU pinning and 64-byte alignment, median of 1000 iterations, per the project README
claimed_speedup: ~183x faster than nlohmann::json on a 25MB array (4,577 MB/s vs 25 MB/s) and ~180x faster on canada.json (5,585 MB/s vs 31 MB/s); ~2.4x faster than simdjson on large arrays; described as 'within 1-2%' of simdjson on 256MB datasets (derived from page's MB/s figures; the nlohmann ratio exceeds the 50x plausibility threshold in the task's own rules)
tradeoffs: Licensed under a proprietary 'TACHYON PROPRIETARY SOURCE LICENSE v1.0' that explicitly prohibits redistribution and modification/extraction of its ASM/SIMD kernels -- code can be studied but not reused or copied. No public benchmark harness file was found alongside the README (numbers appear to be self-run and pasted in, not scripted/reproducible).
caveats: 180x claim is far above the task's 50x implausibility threshold and the repo provides no compiler flags, no committed benchmark code, and only a partial hardware description -- capped at tier C rather than A/B for this reason. Zero GitHub stars; all commits landed in a single day (2026-01-04) via a merge from a 'wilkolbrzym-coder/tachyon-v6-release' branch, suggesting this is the same project originally posted to Show HN under github.com/wilkolbrzym-coder/Tachyon.JSON (that repo now 404s) rather than an independent implementation. Proprietary license means usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.
